sources.claim: A constructor establishes a valid new object by initializing required state, validating arguments, and delegating to another constructor or superclass before ordinary instance use.

canonicalExplanation.summary: A constructor's job is to make sure **no invalid object ever exists**. Initialise every required field, **validate** arguments and throw (`IllegalArgumentException`, `Objects.requireNonNull`) if they can't form a valid object. When a class has several constructors, have the convenience ones **delegate** with `this(...)` as their **first statement**, so validation lives in **one place**. Mark fields `final` when they never change after construction. Java only provides a free **no-argument constructor** if you declare **no constructors at all**; declare any constructor and it's gone.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's Range class has two constructors that each copy the validation code, and one of them forgets to check that min <= max. Later they add a two-argument constructor and existing code calling `new Range()` stops compiling. A two-argument constructor validates normalized bounds, while a convenience constructor delegates with this(...) so the invariant has one implementation. In this lesson you'll implement constructors that prevent invalid observable object state.

sections.heading: The invariant: established once, in one constructor
Validate early

Delegate between constructors with this(...) and explain when the default constructor exists.

examples.title: Two constructors, one validation
examples.situation: A two-argument constructor validates normalized bounds, while a convenience constructor delegates with this(...) so the invariant has one implementation.
walkthrough: **A two-argument constructor validates normalized bounds:** Range(10, 3) stores min 3 and max 10.
**A convenience constructor delegates with this(...):** Range() calls this(0, 0), which calls the main constructor.
**So the invariant has one implementation:** fixing or tightening the check will happen in one place only.
examples.result: Every Range that exists has min <= max.

examples.title: The late null
examples.situation: A Customer constructor accepts a null email, and a crash happens days later when a newsletter job calls email.toLowerCase().
walkthrough: The bad value was accepted at construction.
The exception now points at the code that created the Customer.
examples.result: Bad data is rejected immediately with a clear message.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Java supplies a no-argument constructor even after any constructor is declared, and validation can be postponed safely until the first method call.
misconceptions.correction: The default constructor exists only when a class declares none. Postponed validation lets invalid objects exist and fail far from their cause.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why didn't new Range() compile?

analogy.example: A constructor is like **a factory's final inspection**: nothing leaves the building until it passes. Having every production line **send items through one inspection station** (this(...) delegation) means the rules can't drift apart between lines.
limitations: Factories can recall products; Java objects can't be recalled.
final fields are parts welded in place.

steps.explanation: The two-argument constructor validates and normalises the bounds.
A convenience constructor delegates with this(...), so the invariant has one implementation.
Methods can rely on min <= max without rechecking.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing constructor delegation. Step 1, Normalise: min is 3; max is 10; label is range. The two-argument constructor validates and normalises the bounds. Step 2, Delegate: chain is Range() -> Range(0, 0) -> Range(0, 0, "range"). A convenience constructor delegates with this(...), so the invariant has one implementation. Step 3, Use: contains(5) is true. Methods can rely on min <= max without rechecking.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write a Temperature class storing kelvin with a validating constructor (kelvin >= 0) and a convenience constructor taking celsius that delegates. Test valid, zero and negative inputs.

farTransfer.prompt: Write an Email class whose constructor rejects null, strips whitespace, lowercases, and requires exactly one '@' with text on both sides. Add a delegating constructor, and test at least six valid and invalid inputs.

remediation.explanation: For each class ask: **can any combination of constructor arguments create an invalid object?** If yes, validate it in the single main constructor.

recap.summary: To implement constructors that prevent invalid state, initialise every required field, validate or normalise arguments and throw early, make unchanging fields final, delegate convenience constructors to one main constructor with this(...) as the first statement, and declare a no-arg constructor explicitly when needed.
